02 / PREVENT

Before ignition.
Design for safety.

Material choice, electrical design and airflow work together to reduce fire risk.

Choose materials for the environment.

Heating can break down plastics, textiles and other solid materials, releasing gases and vapours before visible flames appear. This process is called pyrolysis. Material selection therefore considers how a material behaves when heated, not just whether it burns in a familiar Earth environment.

01 / MATERIAL

Test the actual configuration.

Composition, thickness, exposed area and nearby surfaces affect a material’s behaviour. A material name alone does not establish whether an installed component meets fire-safety requirements.

02 / ATMOSPHERE

Consider oxygen and pressure.

Flammability depends on the surrounding atmosphere. Materials must be assessed for the oxygen concentration and pressure of the intended habitat, including relevant operating conditions.

03 / IGNITION

Control sources of heat.

Electrical faults, overheating equipment and damaged components can provide ignition energy. Material screening is one part of prevention alongside electrical and thermal design.

SoFIE investigates ignition and burning of solid materials, including materials relevant to spacecraft interiors. These experiments help explain behaviour; they do not make every tested material suitable for every application.

Ventilation changes the fire environment.

EXPLORE THREE EFFECTS

Ventilation moves air through a cabin and equipment spaces. In microgravity it strongly influences where oxygen and smoke travel because ordinary buoyant rise is greatly reduced. More airflow is not automatically safer: flow can supply oxygen to a flame as well as carry heat and combustion products away.

COOLING

Account for the installed airflow path.

Equipment produces heat. Cooling design must account for how air reaches and leaves the equipment, including obstructions and enclosed spaces.

CONFINED SPACES

Consider concealed flame spread.

In narrow gaps, nearby walls remove heat while incoming air supplies oxygen. Weak flames can persist as separate flamelets under some conditions. A weak or hidden flame is not necessarily extinguished.

DETECTION

Connect ventilation to sensing.

Smoke must reach a detector’s sampling inlet. An airflow path can help transport smoke to a sensor, but this does not guarantee a detection time or coverage of every compartment.

Illustrative airflow. Ventilation responses depend on the vehicle and its procedures.

CREW ENVIRONMENTS / CONDITIONS TO COMPARE

The atmosphere is part of the material test.

The challenge brief describes future lunar habitats and pressurised rovers with higher oxygen concentrations and lower pressures than Earth’s atmosphere. A material tested in one atmosphere may behave differently in another. Oxygen concentration, total pressure and airflow must be recorded separately.

SPACECRAFT & STATIONS

Microgravity and ventilation

Without strong buoyant rise, fans and local flow paths influence oxygen supply, heat transfer and smoke transport. Compare material geometry and airflow as well as the fuel itself.

LUNAR BASES & ROVERS

Oxygen-rich atmospheres

The brief discusses oxygen concentrations of 30% or more at pressures of 10.2 psi or less, compared with about 21% and 14.7 psi at Earth’s sea level. These are challenge assumptions, not a final atmosphere specification or a safe operating range.

MOON & MARS

Partial gravity needs evidence

Surface habitats have partial gravity, not microgravity. The brief identifies LUCI and FM2 as expected sources of future partial-gravity data. Earth and microgravity results can guide questions, but do not establish the result at lunar or Martian gravity.

A higher oxygen fraction can increase flammability. The size of the change depends on pressure, fuel, flow and geometry.

Connecting material tests to spacecraft design

Material test results, atmosphere conditions, installation geometry, equipment heat loads and airflow paths help engineers assess fire prevention together.
